_why: Capability OBSERVATIONS about the three harnesses, each pinned to the version it was measured on. Codex and Antigravity ship almost daily, so a sentence like 'this flag does not exist' is evidence about one build, never a ruling. npm run harness:usage compares measuredOn with the installed version and prints every observation that is now UNVERIFIED, with the probe that re-settles it. A CONSTRAINT is different: it comes from our own rules or a contract we own, does not lapse with a release, and is listed here only so a reader can tell the two apart. Append; never delete - a lapsed observation gets re-measured and its measuredOn moves.

observations.claim: SPLIT BY ACTION on 1.1.28 - it is neither refuted nor true as one sentence, and the two earlier verdicts were both over-general. LISTING NO LONGER AUTO-DENIES: the reprobe call (npm run agy:read, no command grant, "list the files in <dir>") returned a complete directory listing in 6.5 s, CHECKED against the filesystem rather than merely observed to be non-empty - 16 files, every size correct, including one 120 bytes long created four minutes earlier. SEARCH STILL AUTO-DENIES: on the same night and the same build, a repo-wide citation sweep spent 8.8 s and about 18 K tokens and returned an EMPTY response, because a model asked to search reaches for grep_search, which is still not a grantable action (docs/backlog/antigravity-cannot-grep-so-sweeps-routed-to-it-return-nothing.md, ledger label ad-handoff-citation-sweep). So the wrapper's no-command-grant warning is NOT stale - it is right about search and wrong about listing, and should be narrowed rather than removed. ROUTING CONSEQUENCE: never send Antigravity a task whose question is "find every file that mentions X", because the enumeration is the answer rather than the input; enumerate the files yourself and it reads them faultlessly. The earlier refutations, on 1.1.27 and on the first 1.1.28 pass, each probed ONE action and generalised - the same mistake this file records under the subagent-notification correction. Previously refuted on 1.1.27 (2026-09-09) without the accuracy check, and measured true on 1.1.25 (2026-09-03): headless agy auto-denied any tool with no grant and still returned status SUCCESS with an empty response; only read_file, command and write_file were real grant actions (list_dir, grep_search, codebase_search were accepted into settings.json and dropped as invalid).
observations.reprobe: TWO calls, and one alone answers nothing. (1) With no command grant, ask it to LIST a directory: an accurate listing means listing is allowed. (2) With no command grant, ask it to FIND every file containing a string: an empty response means search is still auto-denied. Record the two separately; the actions do not move together.
observations.source: docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md, "Three facts about this machine that were not true when this file last said them"; refuted by the 2026-09-09 capability re-probe, commit 1a51192f

observations.claim: Codex writes a rate_limits snapshot into its rollout only when one of its own sessions runs, so the capacity reading can be absent or stale; availability is three-valued (headroom / low / UNKNOWN) and is never probed with a paid call.
observations.reprobe: npm run harness:usage after a Codex session; the snapshot line names its own timestamp.

observations.claim: An Agent call with isolation: "remote" is ACCEPTED and runs on this laptop anyway, in an ordinary local worktree (hostname Legion-001, win32, .claude/worktrees/agent-<id>). The launch reports success and nothing says the isolation was dropped, so a wave routing rows to "cloud" spends the local RAM it meant to save while the plan still reads as honoured.

observations.claim: PARTLY REFUTED, then CORRECTED the same day on 2.1.263. The routing is neither 'always the launcher' nor 'always the session': a subagent's completion notification goes to WHOEVER IS INSIDE A TURN when it fires. Measured both ways. (a) Two probes had a launched session spawn a subagent and stay inside a turn - one explicitly sat in a 120-second blocking command - and the notification arrived in that session, carrying the subagent's final message verbatim. (b) A controlled probe had a launched session spawn one background subagent and END ITS TURN immediately; that notification arrived in the LAUNCHER, and the marker file confirmed the subagent had run, so 'no notification' is not confounded with 'never ran'. (c) In the field, sixteen fan-out reports have strayed to a launcher: seven from one row on 2026-09-08 and eight from another on 2026-09-09. A FAN-OUT IS ALWAYS CASE (b), because a session that has spawned agents has nothing left to do but end its turn and wait - which is why waiting on one never works and why the original observation held in practice for the case that matters. The earlier note here, that this was simply 'REFUTED', was measured correctly and generalised wrongly from the stay-in-turn case alone. Consequence for a launcher: stray reports belong to the row that spawned them - relay them with scripts/relay.mjs rather than acting on them. Previously measured true on 2.1.240 (2026-09-03): a session launched by another session never receives its own subagents' completion notifications; they route to the launcher.
observations.reprobe: Two probes, and they must be run as a PAIR or the answer is half true. From a launched session: (1) spawn a background subagent and stay inside one long blocking call - the notification should arrive in that session at the turn boundary; (2) spawn one and end the turn immediately - it should arrive in the launcher. Confirm the subagent actually ran via a marker file in both cases.
observations.source: .agent-workflows/orchestrator/incidents.md, "the fan-out that waited on notifications that could not arrive"; refuted by the 2026-09-09 capability re-probe, commit 1a51192f

observations.claim: PARTIALLY REFUTED as of 2.1.263: `claude agents --json` still answers in under a second with pid and cwd, but the objects no longer carry a status field at all (kind, startedAt and sessionId appear instead) - anything reading `status` off this command now reads undefined rather than a stale or wrong value. Previously measured true on 2.1.251 (2026-09-03): claude agents --json answered in under a second with pid, cwd and status, and was the third liveness signal beside the two transcript-based ones.
observations.reprobe: node scripts/claude-agents.mjs; it probes the command's shape on every run and degrades to unknown by itself. A `status` in the raw `claude agents --json` output confirms the original claim; its absence confirms the refutation.
observations.source: .agent-workflows/orchestrator/incidents.md, "the third liveness signal"; refuted by the 2026-09-09 capability re-probe, commit 1a51192f

observations.claim: scripts/agy-run.mjs refuses --dangerously-skip-permissions rather than forwarding it, and a write runs only in a linked worktree on a feature branch. This is our rule, not a fact about agy, and it does not lapse with a release.

A Codex row always names a fallback pool, because Codex capacity is shared with the owner's other projects and can be near zero on a given day. Codex is otherwise available by default (owner, 2026-09-03) - this constrains the plan's shape, not how much Codex it uses.

CONFIRMED with one correction on 0.154.0-alpha.11, re-derived from scratch by a controlled pair of delegations four minutes apart from one session. The writable set is THE LAUNCHING SESSION'S WORKING DIRECTORY PLUS THE TEMP DIRECTORIES, not the working directory alone. Probe A wrote a file under the launching session's own worktree and got every fact in it right. Probe B, same launcher and same flags, was handed two targets in one run: a path in a SIBLING WORKTREE was refused, and the refusal on this build is an OS access error, not a sandbox policy message - verbatim, `New-Item : Access to the path 'C:\claude\NoaCG-Studio\.claude\worktrees\new-session-db1287\.codex-probe-b.txt' is denied.` - while a path under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp in the SAME RUN succeeded. Both outcomes were checked on disk. The mechanism is printed by Codex itself on every run and needs no probing at all: the startup banner of `codex exec` reads `sandbox: workspace-write [workdir, /tmp, $TMPDIR]`. Consequence for a reader of this entry: the temp directory is writable, so a delegation can stage a file it cannot place, and a session that only reads the summary can record a task as attempted while nothing moved. Everything below still holds. A delegation's writable root is THE LAUNCHING SESSION'S WORKING DIRECTORY, and nothing else outside temp. Measured three times on 2026-09-09, and the third attempt CONFIRMS the rule by succeeding. First, handed the ordinary row recipe ('make a feature branch in its own worktree before the work starts'), the delegate was denied writing C:/claude/NoaCG-Studio/.git/refs/heads/<branch> and stopped having changed no file. Then, given a worktree created for it in advance and told to run no git at all, it refused again and said why in plain terms: the target 'is outside that writable root, and approval is disabled', naming the launching session's own worktree as the only writable path. It read both target files correctly and reported its analysis, so reads are unrestricted; only writes are pinned. CONSEQUENCE FOR ROUTING: pre-creating a worktree does NOT help, because the root follows the launcher, not the prompt. A delegation can only edit files under the directory the launching session is sitting in. Either launch it from a session whose cwd IS the worktree the work belongs in, or have it edit in the launcher's own checkout and move the result. Third attempt, launched from a session whose OWN working directory was the target worktree: it created a new module and edited three existing files there without complaint. So the rule is positive as well as negative - delegate from the session that sits where the result belongs and it simply works. This is the mechanical reason such delegations get recorded as attempted and never landed, and it is not fixed by choosing the harness more often.
observations.reprobe: Cheapest first: run any `codex exec` and read the `sandbox:` line of its startup banner, which names the writable set outright. To re-derive it, delegate ONE run that attempts two writes - one into a different worktree, one into the temp directory - and asks for each outcome separately; check both on disk rather than believing the report.
observations.source: docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md - the delegate that cannot make its own branch; re-derived and corrected by the 2026-09-09 harness verdict, docs/metrics/2026-09-09-harness-verdict.md

observations.claim: Every `codex exec` starts a fleet of node processes that does NOT exit when the run does, and the cost is memory rather than time. Measured on this laptop: 10 node processes and 619 MB before any delegation, 40 processes and 2554 MB after four wrapper delegations and five plain `codex exec` runs, with codex.exe going from one process to three. Not every invocation leaves a whole family behind, so do not divide those totals: the firm per-delegation figure is the REAP, which freed 778 MB by killing the sixteen processes belonging to four completed delegations - four processes and about 195 MB each. The survivors group by creation time into families of five to seven processes measuring 330-430 MB AT CREATION - a cua_node launch.mjs, an ./mcp/server.mjs, a staging runtime, and an npx `@playwright/mcp` pair worth about 175 MB of it - and each family stays resident long after its own job completes; the oldest on screen was 40 minutes past its work. Budget 195 MB per delegation as the residue and treat 330-430 MB as the peak. The parents are ALIVE, not orphaned: one codex.exe (pid 4264) was holding four separate fleets, one per session it had served. TWO CONSEQUENCES FOR ROUTING. First, this is NOT the delegation wrapper's doing - two of the leaked families came from plain `codex exec` with no wrapper involved, because the three MCP servers are declared globally in ~/.codex/config.toml, so the orchestrator's only contribution is calling Codex more often than a person does. Second, STARTUP is not the problem and should stop being blamed: the whole MCP fleet is worth 1.1-1.4 s (6.78 s with `-c mcp_servers="{}"` against 7.90-8.19 s with it) and exactly zero tokens (12,443 either way), and the wrapper's channel adds about 3 s to an 8 s job.
observations.reprobe: Count node processes and their total working set before and after a `codex exec`, then group the survivors by creation time and check each family's parent with Get-CimInstance Win32_Process. A family still resident after its job's completedAt confirms it.
observations.source: docs/metrics/2026-09-09-harness-verdict.md, question 4; independently corroborated the same night by claude/ab-reap-codex-delegation-tree, which measured 30 processes and 1.4 GB from three delegations that had ended hours earlier

observations.claim: The Agent tool takes `isolation` (worktree or remote) but no working-directory parameter, so a new subagent starts either in a FRESH worktree or in the launcher's own checkout - never in an existing worktree. And no SendMessage is callable from a main session: the Agent tool's own description tells you to use SendMessage to continue an agent, but the tool is not in the session's tool list. Together they mean an orchestrator can neither ADOPT a dead row's worktree nor WAKE the row that owns it. Measured on row CA of the 2026-09-10 night wave: it stalled holding the only copy of the rebuilt 25 September deck as uncommitted files in its worktree, and the rescue had to be a new row that copied the files out by path into its own branch.
observations.reprobe: Read the Agent tool's parameter schema for a cwd or working-directory field, and the session's tool list for SendMessage. Either one present refutes the matching half; record the halves separately.
observations.source: the 2026-09-11 deck rescue, `docs/DEMO_2026-09-25.md` beat O2 and the commit that rebuilt the deck
